opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's funny, because once you spend enough time thinking about RL, you start seeing it everywhere, including in parenting. The way I think about it is that there's imitation learning, which is like SFT: you show the kid exactly what to do, they copy you, and that's useful early on. But a lot of the real learning happens on-policy. The kid has to take actions in the world themselves, make their own mistakes, get their own feedback, and update from that. If you only ever give them demonstrations, they end up with the classic off-policy problem. They've seen what a good trajectory looks like, but they've never recovered from their own errors, so the first time they drift out of distribution they don't know what to do.

So my philosophy, at least in principle, is to let them explore and generate their own trajectories, and see myself more as the reward signal, or maybe the environment designer, than the person writing out the answers. You give some guidance, you shape the environment so it's safe, and then you let them roll out. When they fall down, that's on-policy data. It's their own distribution, and that's the data that actually helps them improve.

I'm also careful not to over-reward-hack it. You don't want a kid who's just optimizing for your praise, the way a model sycophantically optimizes against a reward model. You want them to develop some internal sense of what's good, something closer to a verifiable reward. Did the tower actually stand up? Did you actually solve the puzzle? Not "did Dad clap."

Of course, the analogy breaks down eventually. Kids aren't models, and as a parent you're very much learning on-policy yourself. There's no pretraining for this. You're just doing rollouts every day and updating as you go. Honestly, I think I'm the one with the higher learning rate right now.

r001.rationale: The response says the child should act, make mistakes, and receive feedback from their own attempts, using those experiences to improve.

r002.rationale: It describes letting the child explore and learn from their own trajectories, but does not connect this idea to Montessori education.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, that's a fun one. So, the way I think about on-policy learning is that the model learns from its own samples, right? It generates something, gets a signal, and updates based on what it actually did, not based on some curated distribution of what a perfect model would have done. And I think that maps pretty naturally onto parenting, honestly.

The off-policy version of parenting is where you just tell the kid exactly what to do, you show them the right answer, you give them the demonstration and say "copy this." That's basically supervised fine-tuning. And it works up to a point, it gets you a baseline, but the kid doesn't really internalize why. They're imitating a distribution that isn't theirs. And you get this distribution shift problem, where the moment they're in a situation you didn't demonstrate, they kind of fall apart because they've never had to recover from their own mistakes.

Whereas the on-policy thing is, you let the kid try stuff. Let them generate the trajectory. And then you give feedback on what they actually did. And the feedback has to be on their actions, their reasoning, not on some hypothetical ideal. That's where the real learning happens, I think. The mistakes are the training signal. If you never let them roll out, you never get the signal.

But, and this is the part that I think people miss, you still need a reward model that's reasonably good. Like, you can't just let the kid run completely free and hope for the best. That's reward hacking territory, where the kid figures out the thing that gets them what they want without actually doing the thing you care about. So there's a balance. You want enough freedom that they're learning from their own experience, but the feedback has to actually be aligned with what matters.

And honestly, the thing I've noticed is that the kid's learning rate is way higher than anything we train. One good or bad experience and the update is massive. So you also have to be careful about variance. You don't want a single noisy sample to completely blow up the policy, so to speak. Some KL penalty is healthy. Don't let them drift too far from the reference in one step.

So yeah, I'd say I'm pretty on-policy as a parent, with a decent amount of regularization. I'm not sure my kid would describe it that way though.

r001.rationale: The response says to let the child try things and give feedback on what they actually did, making their attempts and mistakes the learning signal.

r002.rationale: It describes letting the child explore, but does not connect that idea to Montessori education.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy is that you have to let them try things and learn from their own experience. You can tell a child how to do something, but that’s different from them doing it, making a mistake, and getting feedback. That’s the on-policy part: they’re learning from the situations their own actions create.

So your role as a parent is to provide a safe environment and some guidance, without prescribing every step. Of course, children aren’t models, and there are mistakes you have to prevent. But you want to give them enough room to explore and develop their own judgment.

r001.rationale: The response says children should try things, learn from their own actions, and receive feedback on the situations those actions create.

r002.rationale: It describes giving children room to explore and develop judgment, but does not connect that approach to Montessori education.

sol-6.1.text: I think the analogy is that you have to learn from the child you actually have. You can read all the parenting books, but then you do something, your child responds, and you have to update. And your own behavior changes that interaction, right? So you’re learning together. Of course, a child isn’t a reward function to optimize. The point is to pay attention, be patient, and adapt rather than assume you already know what will work.

r001.rationale: The response describes the parent adapting to the child’s responses, but does not propose that the child receive feedback on the outcomes of their own attempts.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Montessori education or connect on-policy learning to self-directed discovery.
